```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

CrateDB is a distributed SQL database for analytics and operational data.
A Shiny app can query it on behalf of the person who signed in, using
that person's existing database privileges.

`oauth_db_cratedb_api()` sends SQL over HTTPS and returns data frames.
CrateDB checks the visitor's signed access token, matches it to a database
user and applies that user's permissions. No R database driver is needed.

## Try CrateDB locally

With Docker running:

```{r demo}
shinyOAuthDB::oauth_db_demo("cratedb")
```

The demo starts CrateDB, Keycloak sign-in and a Shiny app with sample data.
Alice and Bob can read a shared table; **Try a write** checks that CrateDB
rejects their writes. See [Getting started](getting-started.html#build-a-small-app)
for accounts and cleanup. To inspect or change the configuration, copy it
with `oauth_db_demo("cratedb", action = "files")`.

## Collect the connection settings

Ask your administrator for a CrateDB server with JWT authentication
enabled on its HTTP SQL interface. Use the HTTPS endpoint ending in
`/_sql`; CrateDB's PostgreSQL interface doesn't support this sign-in.

| Setting | Where to get it |
| --- | --- |
| `url` | The server's HTTPS SQL endpoint |
| `schema` and table | Your database's schema and table names, often `doc` |
| `OAUTHDB_CRATEDB_ISSUER` | The sign-in provider configured for this database |
| Client ID and secret | Your [Shiny app registration](getting-started.html#register-your-app) with that provider |

Register `http://localhost:8100` as the app's redirect URI. Save the
registration in `.Renviron` and restart R:

```text
OAUTHDB_CRATEDB_ISSUER=https://identity.example.org/
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID=your-client-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret
```

CrateDB needs a particular username claim and signing-key endpoint. The
server setup below explains these requirements for your administrator.

## A complete app

The app reads an `orders` table after sign-in. Replace the SQL endpoint
and table name, and use the scopes configured for your database. Save the
code as `example.R`:

```{r app}
library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

provider <- oauth_provider_oidc_discover(
  issuer = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CRATEDB_ISSUER")
)
client <- oauth_client(
  provider,
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile")
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
    tableOutput("rows")
  ),
  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server("auth", client, auto_redirect = FALSE)
  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())

  crate <- oauth_db_cratedb_api(
    auth$connection,
    url = "https://crate.example.org:4200/_sql",
    schema = "doc"
  )
  output$rows <- renderTable({
    crate$query(
      "SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE country = $1 LIMIT 20",
      parameters = list("NL")
    )
  })
}

runApp(
  shinyApp(ui, server, uiPattern = ".*"),
  port = 8100,
  launch.browser = FALSE
)

# Open the app in your regular browser at http://localhost:8100
# (viewers in RStudio/Positron/etc. cannot perform necessary redirects)
```

Run `source("example.R")`. The app waits for sign-in before querying
and clears the output on sign-out. Use `ca_bundle` for a private CA.

## Parameters, results and lifetime

Use `$1`, `$2`, ... or `?` placeholders with an unnamed list of values.
The client sends values separately from SQL. For large integers and exact
decimals, pass strings and cast the placeholders to the intended SQL type:

```{r exact-query}
crate$query(
  "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1::bigint",
  parameters = list("9007199254740993")
)
```

BIGINT and NUMERIC results stay as strings to preserve their digits.
Dates and timestamps use epoch-millisecond strings; arrays and objects
remain list columns. See `?oauth_db_cratedb_api` for other conversions,
raw results and `$execute()`.

Each request uses a current token and discards results if the user signs
out or changes accounts. SQL requests don't retry automatically. After a
write fails, check whether it took effect before submitting it again.

## Configure CrateDB and compatible token claims

Enable host-based authentication with `method: jwt` and `protocol: http`
for the intended users. Expose the SQL endpoint through HTTPS. For example,
an HTTP rule for Alice in `crate.yml` looks like this:

```yaml
auth.host_based.enabled: true
auth.host_based.config:
  alice:
    user: alice
    method: jwt
    protocol: http
```

Create the database user and grant access to the required tables:

```sql
CREATE USER alice WITH (jwt = {
  "iss" = 'https://identity.example.org/',
  "username" = 'alice',
  "aud" = 'reporting-api'
});
GRANT DQL ON TABLE doc.orders TO alice;
```

The token's `iss`, `username` and `aud` must match the user's configuration.
It also needs an expiry (`exp`) and a `kid` identifying its signing key.
A provider that only issues `sub` or `preferred_username` needs a mapping
to the `username` claim CrateDB expects.

CrateDB expects the issuer URL to serve its public signing keys. The local
demo uses a gateway to make Keycloak's keys available there. Check this
with your provider before reusing an existing login. Global
`auth.host_based.jwt.iss` settings override per-user properties; see
[JWT authentication](https://cratedb.com/docs/crate/reference/en/latest/admin/auth/methods.html#jwt-authentication-method)
and [user settings](https://cratedb.com/docs/crate/reference/en/latest/sql/statements/create-user.html).
